en: **The Eight Verses on Caṇḍikā** We worship the excellent Maheśa, who takes refuge in the great mind, whose splendor brings about supreme prosperity—He who fills the quarters with masses of moonlight more beautiful than a thousand moons, who drives away the stubbornness of the Kali age, and whose stainless body is adorned by the female crane. [We worship] this delightful Kapālinī, the protectress of the three worlds, who delights in dwelling within the vast interior of mountain caves.

We worship Umā, the Great Goddess, who is served by the gods, the supreme mother of Gaṇeśvara, the daughter of the Lord of Mountains. (2) O Great Mistress! These gods, headed by Mahendra, together bring the pollen from their feet to the crowns of their heads. I meditate in my mind upon that Ummā, who is clothed in space, who is praised, and who is devoted to Śaṅkara—the Great Passionless One—though she herself is full of passion for him. (3) I worship her, the destroyer of the sorrow of her own world, whose hair is stirred by the swaying, beautiful chowries rising from the hands of the celestial damsels.

[We praise] her who has made the Lord (Īśvara) a supreme expert in the *tāṇḍava* dance, set in motion by an abundance of graceful movements born from no small measure of intense agitation. Even here, having made the common man a *cāmara* (fly-whisk), and likewise the immortal one non-aging (*nupāmara*), she whose threefold nature is manifested by the glance of the Supreme Lord proceeds with the play of both pleasure and anger for the sake of destroying one's own faults; we bow to her who attains the union of prosperity. O you who shine, illuminating the sky and its depths with a mass of radiant splendor, you appear everywhere, pervading the worlds with your light.

I worship her whose forehead-plate is illuminated by the mass of light emitted from the fire that blazes, glows, and intensely burns upon it; I worship Kapālikāminī, whose neck is as beautiful as a pigeon or a conch shell, adorned with lovely bracelets, armlets, and other ornaments, and who possesses the exceptional skill of a poet arising from the production of the sound of the anklets on her excellent feet; I worship Kapālakuṇḍalā. || 6–7 ||

O Bhavānī, you who manifest fearlessness from worldly existence, you who transcend existence through your radiance, O worthy one, you who contemplate the splendor of the spiritual stages, you who are the source of abundance—O Bhavānī, I worship your lotus feet, where enemies do not exist and where there is no perception of such things. (8) Whoever recites this hymn to Bhavānī, composed by Umāpati before Durgā, which is most profound in its majesty and auspicious in nature, shall attain the fortune of sovereignty over the city of Indra; for him, even his enemies will become as mere blades of grass. (9)

This hymn was offered on the eighth day of the bright fortnight of Āśvina, on a Thursday, in the year reckoned as Rāma (3), Aṣṭa (8), and Aṅka (9)—that is, 1983—by Śākta-Śrī-Jagadānanda Śarman. Thus ends the Caṇḍikāṣṭaka composed by the venerable Umāpati Dvivedin, whose secondary name is Kavipati.
